title: "Material uncertainty" hangs over the future of Life is Strange developers Don't Nod beyond January 2027, as negotiations over potential layoffs begin
author: Mark Warren
content:
Up to 90 staff at the Lost Records: Bloom and Rage studio could be axed soon

Life is Strange developers Don't Nod have acknowledged that there's "material uncertainty regarding the company's ability to continue as a going concern beyond January 31st, 2027", as they kick off negotiations with the union representing staff who could be laid off as part of a "transformation project". The proposed cuts, which could see up to 90 jobs eliminated, are the latest development in the studio's efforts to make their financial future look less like a road to ruin which might run its course either this year or very early in 2027.

As spotted by our suit-wearing colleagues at Gamesindustry.biz, Don't Nod posted their financial results for the first half of 2026 late last week, providing a bit more information on the plans they're putting in motion to start trying to turn things around by likely laying a bunch of people off.

"Consolidated gross cash at the end of June 2026 amounted to €9.8 million and €8.0 million at the end of July 2026, compared to €15.4 million at the end of 2025," the company wrote. "Given the available cash and the cash flow forecast, the company's ability to continue operations depends partly on securing external financing to cover business operation and project development needs. This represents material uncertainty regarding the company's ability to continue as a going concern beyond January 31st, 2027."

As for the proposed layoffs as Don't Nod scramble to right the ship, the studio noted that "up to 90 positions" might be affected. The company's management have already begun negotiations with the union representing staff, after their board of directors have approved the "transformation" plans. The stated goal of those plans as of right now is a "refocusing" of Don't Nod's operations in France "around a single production line, bringing together the expertise required to launch new projects before the completion of current productions". The company claim this'll mean "priority projects" will get more attention, while resource allocation and responsibilities will be clearer.

In the meantime, Don't Nod are "continuing to examine the most appropriate legal and operational arrangements to support this transformation and ensure the continuity of [their] operations, in the best interests of all [their] stakeholders". "The measures being considered today are difficult; we fully appreciate what they may mean for the employees affected and are ensuring that the necessary support measures are put in place," CEO Oskar Guilbert put it. "This plan is, however, essential to ensuring the Company's continued operations."

Solidarity with any Don't Nod workers devs who end up being affected, if the studio do end up laying staff off. .

title: "You may be overthinking it a little bit": Tim Willits doesn't think Rideshare's generative AI is damaging Saber's reputation
author: Julian Benson
content:
Stimulating conversation

A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z, the company was dealing with the shitstorm that ensued from their announcement of Rideshare Stimulator.

The game's basically an Uber simulator, with you driving a car around town picking up fares, but Saber drew all kinds of bad attention when a former writer on the game revealed the game featured generative AI (something left undisclosed on the game's Steam page until recently) and CEO Matt Karch responded by attacking the writer in statements to the press. Something he has since apologised for.

So, naturally, we talked about generative AI and the reputational damage – or lack of – when getting caught out using it.

Rideshare will have a main narrative, similar to other simulator games, in which you start your business in a city and grow it up as you complete jobs. Similar to something you would play through in Snowrunner. "All that is written by humans, all the missions are written by humans," Willits tells me. Where the generative AI appears is in Rideshare's Free Ride mode.

In Free Ride, when you pick up a fare, their dialogue will be generated using an LLM. "What we want to do is feed current events, like maybe there's some soccer game, and some ride will get in and talk about it," Willits explains. He says Saber are "using it here in a small part of a small game to test the waters." and that the company are "interested in how AI can help in games."

Willits says Rideshare is the only game in which Saber are using generative AI – "We don't have AI in Space Marine. We don't have AI in Hellraiser. We don't have AI in Jurassic Park, but we want to figure it out and we want to try something."

When I spoke with Willits, the thing I most wanted to know was why there was no AI disclosure on the Rideshare's Steam page when it was first revealed. Valve have a clear policy on disclosing the use of generative AI both in the production of a game and if any feature of the game makes ongoing calls to LLMs.

The reason, Willits says, is they "had an announce plan, but that got a little sideways". There was going to be a sneak peak, then there would have been reveals of the game's features in the future, and as part of that the generative technology would have been revealed. To indicate how early in the game's reveal rollout they are, Willits points out Rideshare's "not here" at Gamescom. "Unfortunately, we had some people talk about the game when they weren't supposed to be talking about the game and that just kind of escalated."

Though, I bring it back to Valve's AI disclosure policy because it doesn't make a distinction between whether a feature has been announced or not, only whether the technology is used in a game. Shouldn't the disclosure still have been there when the game was announced? "Okay, sure," Willits says.

The point I'm building to with Willits is that by not initially disclosing the use of AI, it seeds doubt about generative AI's use in Saber's other games. The tool may have been used but the company is not yet ready to announce or reveal it. I point to another of Saber's games, Road Kings, a new American trucking simulator which I really enjoyed at a preview event in April. While on the road, other drivers or job brokers may message you to ask for help, spurring an emergent quest. Certainly, there's no suggestion that these quests are generated by AI, but to a player the two systems could appear similar and they may now question 'Is this generative AI Saber's not copped to yet?'. "You may be overthinking it a little bit," Willits says. "I wouldn't worry about that. Again, the wishlists are up, interest is up, preorders across our games are up."

I didn't want to move on immediately, as Road Kings captures the issue well. I saw the game back in April but its embargo for the preview only came up after the Rideshare story had broken. I played and enjoyed that game and its mix of American Truck Simulator-style hauling blended with scenes you might see in a disaster move like Twister. But the comments on the preview were largely about the Rideshare news and Saber's use of AI. Willits, again, disagrees this is an issue. "I wouldn't really worry about that," he says. "The games will speak for themselves. You enjoyed Road Kings. The people that play it, they will enjoy it. I've been in the industry for 30 whatever years, you will always get crazy comments."

Willits points back to when he was working at id and they announced Quake 3 would need a video card to play. "We were roasted," he says. "The internet hate was crazy. 'You're ruining the industry. How can you make me pay $100 for a video card?' – imagine a $100 video card! – But the game came out and people liked it."

Willits also points to the launch of Steam, which, while a well-regarded platform now, was not universally loved at launch. In part because its servers struggled and its online functionality demanded more from peoples' internet than a lot of dial up and early broadband connections could provide. "I think we're in a period now of technology change that people are really unsure about," Willits says. "We, as game developers, don't really know what we're doing with it yet. Players don't really know what's going on with it. But I do think that there will be a game from somebody that will be so awesome that everyone will be like 'That's it. Now I get it.' I think the games will speak for themselves and when people play or they read your stories, and they watch the videos and they see the content, they will make their own determination."

As I've said in the past to other developers, I can believe there are ways these new AI technologies could benefit my work. For instance, the first transcription pass of most my interviews is done automatically because I use Google's Recorder app. But I also know the worst thing I could do with [insert AI tool of your choice] would be to generate an article for RPS. No one comes to this site to see something cobbled together by an LLM, they want something lovingly stitched together by these dyslexic typo-spewing hands. So I ask Willits what he thinks the benefit for Saber will be.

"As a game developer, if you're going to try something with brand new generative AI, it's much better to try it with something small [rather] than your biggest title," Willits says. "For us, part of our strategy at Saber is to make our mega hits – Space Marine 3, Jurassic Park, Turok – but we have to have smaller games that are consistent when it comes to how long it takes to make, how much money they make, [that's where] we experiment with things. Look at Spintires. That was an experiment that turned into a mega franchise. Rideshare fits into that category. It is a Rideshare simulator, where you drive around and you pick people up. There's really not much more you can really do there. And so for us, we wanted to be like 'Well, let's try this. Let's try it here because if it doesn't work out, it's on that game. It's not on our mega hits.'"

In the case of Rideshare's Free Ride mode, Willits says "This is a gameplay feature that is not possible without this technology. It would be logistically too hard, it'd be so expensive. We'd have to have an army." And, as he's described it, a mode where passenger dialogue is generated in response to current events fed into the game, I agree. Either you would have a madlibs style system of words being swapped in and out of repeating schemas, or a human writer adding additional lines in response to real world news events.

I do want to see if Saber are able to produce anything better than the other games that have stuck LLMs inside the throats of their characters. In Where Winds Meet, players quickly convinced one of the NPCs that they were pregnant, and another to provide cooking advice for potatoes and ketchup. That implementation and others were panned by developers Samuel Horti spoke to back in December.

My experience of generative AI dialogue has largely been formulaic and predictable. Which, could make for incredibly dreary car journeys. Ironically, the last taxi ride I was in I told the driver he was taking us to an engagement meal and he told me how AI was going to destroy the world by 2030.

Travel and accommodation to Gamescom was provided by the conference organisers.

title: "We’re going to become the new legend": Naoki Hamaguchi on making Final Fantasy 7 Revelation as if it's the last ever Final Fantasy 7 game
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
"That’s why I’ve got this confidence"

In this IP-obsessed world, it is quite easy to wonder if anything will ever actually come to an end. Theoretically, the Final Fantasy 7 trilogy of remakes will be coming to an end next year with Final Fantasy 7 Revelation. Except that might not even be true because a couple of pieces of DLC, about Sephiroth and Vincent Valentine respectively, are also in the works, so who knows when the actual end date is. Whether this is actually the end of Final Fantasy 7 or not, however, doesn't matter, as its director is treating it that way.

"I’m approaching the development of Revelation as if there’s never going to be another Final Fantasy 7 game… no spin-offs… no DLC in the future ," director Naoki Hamaguchi said in a recent interview with Kotaku. "I’m not going to say whether there actually is or not," he continues, making it seem like this interview was probably held before the confirmation of DLC. "But we’re making it as if everything we have for Final Fantasy 7 is going to be put into this game. That’s why I’ve got this confidence, and I think we’re going to beat the original’s legend. We’re going to become the new legend."

That last bit is potentially a slightly strange one, as I'm not sure if one of the most beloved JRPGs of all time can be beaten out by a trilogy of remakes that (while I've personally loved) do suffer from the curse of being a triple-A game in the 2020s. In any case, I was also interested to hear what Hamaguchi had to say on the themes of the threequel: "Yet one other thing that working on the Remake project really brought home is thinking about its other very current-feeling themes. Final Fantasy 7 has a lot of diversity.

"These days, those are big topics and everyone is aware of them; social media gives everyone access to that information. But thinking back, Final Fantasy 7 was way ahead of its time when the original was made. Especially in Japan, finding information about things happening abroad back then was not easy. To think that Mr. Kitase and the team put together a game where you see diversity—the variation between party characters, cultures, and people around the world—30-something years ago makes my respect for him even higher."

Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is due for release on April 8th, 2027.

title: Steam Frame review: Another best-in-class VR headset by Valve, though virtual realities clash with economic ones
author: @rockpapershot
content:
It’s a strange time to be selling a new VR headset, and maybe an even stranger time to be buying one. The supply of original virtual reality games has slowed to a dribble, and just as with Valve’s last hardware launch, the Steam Frame arrives covered in bumps and scrapes from a fight with the worst components shortage in memory. A fight which, judging by how it’ll cost ya £889 / $1,059 at minimum, it lost.

However, something else the Frame has in common with the revamped Steam Machine is that as a piece of hardware per se, it’s really quite likeable. Charismatic, even. It’s a happy marriage of core VR capability and genuinely new engineering ideas: some simple practicality boons, some with the potential to change PC games as we know them. And not just the ones you’d play with sweaty goggles on your face.

These ambitions aren’t necessarily apparent from the moment you lift the Frame (and its two controllers) from the box, but it still makes a good first impression. Despite being a fully wireless, battery-powered kit, it’s lighter, more compact, and far easier to set up than its cabled and base-stationed Valve Index ancestor. Its two 2,160x2,160 LCD lenses also make for a tidy sharpness upgrade, while narrowly edging the overall resolution of the Frame’s sworn enemy: the similarly cable-cutting Meta Quest 3. Prescription lens inserts are being made by Zenni Optical, but I can just about find a comfortable fit for my fairly hefty glasses, so fellow four-eyes – unless you’ve got Farnsworth-spec specs – probably won’t need them.

The Frame’s controllers do lack the hyper-accurate finger tracking of the Index’s, a quality their capacitive sensors are only partially successful in trying to recreate. Otherwise, though, they don’t feel like downgrades. Their inside-out tracking is plenty accurate, and although the adoption of a more gamepad-style, XYAB 'n' D-pad layout was done with playing 'flat' games in mind – more on that later – there’s something comfortable and immediate about using VR controllers with the same inputs as a conventional gamepad. Borrowing the grippy, drift-resistant tunnelling magnetoresistance (TMR) thumbsticks from the new Steam Controller was an especially wise move.

Passthrough play, where onboard cameras feed a view of your surroundings to use as game backdrops, is relatively basic. It’s fine for a few quick rounds of 3D puzzlebuilder Cubism, but the Frame’s monochrome cams represent one of the few areas where the clearer, full-colour Quest 3 has it beat. I’m not personally too fussed about this, mind – you can ask Meta themselves how well whole mixed reality Metaverse thing went, and the Frame’s video quality is fine for, say, quick trips out of the play area to retrieve a vibrating phone.

I hear that that a third-party, colour camera accessory is also in the words, though the usefulfulness of Steam Frame feature this relies on – its modularity – is difficult to assess in its earliest days. It sounds great on paper: besides staples like lens inserts, the idea is that you can swap out parts of it – the strap, the speakers, the battery, the facepad, to name a few – and replace them with more advanced or comfortable modules. Still, how valuable this will be depends on the available modules, and at the time of writing (a few hours before launch) the only add-ons to be officially confirmed are those of Valve’s own Ergonomic Accessories Kit, a pack of improved straps for the controllers and headset.

Happily, the Frame gets flexible and functional well before you’ll feel the need to start yanking bits out of it. Much of this flexibility derives from an exceptionally thoughtful balance of streaming and standalone usage, to the point where the Frame doesn’t feel as if it favours one VR style even as it excels in both.

Thus, streaming from a PC – your best bet for maximum visual fidelity – is helped along by a number of honest-to-goodness tech innovations. Foveated streaming, for one, makes use of the Frame’s eye tracking (itself an entire feature that both the Index and Quest 3 lack) to only stream a full-quality image where you’re currently looking at. Peripheral vision areas are streamed in lower quality to save bandwidth and, by extension, keep performance high. The transition between the two qualities is near enough instantaneous, so I couldn’t perceive it happening unless I stopped to look for it.

Where most wireless VR headsets also stream via a WiFi router rather than a PC, increasing latency, the Frame also takes a shortcut by streaming straight from a USB dongle. In the same room, this is as quick as any wired headset I’ve ever worn, but the Frame goes one further by combining both dongle and Wi-Fi connectivity into one consistent air tether: if you’re far enough away from your PC that the dongle and Wi-Fi are jostling for a performance lead, the headset will automatically (and, as far as I can tell, seamlessly) switch between whichever is faster in the moment. It’s a clever boost to the Frame’s stability and range alike, and while results will vary from setup to setup, I only started noticing lag when dragging the Frame two walls and two doors away from both PC and router. And even then, it was still broadly playable.

Standalone mode, meanwhile, is handled by a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor, 16GB of that gold dust RAM, and whatever games you fancy whacking on the Frame’s 256GB or 1TB SSDs. Or, indeed, a microSD card – you can actually hot-swap Steam games installs on the same card across a Frame, Steam Machine, and Steam Deck, another nice touch.

All the same, some expectation-tempering goes a long way here; that Snapdragon is a modest upgrade on the Quest 3’s equivalent, but it’s still a smartphone chip, and standalone games often exhibit lower animation quality and/or fuzzier rendering resolutions than their streamed equivalents. Then again, there are also games where the difference, even if visible, is immaterial. Big VR hitters like SuperHot and Beat Saber still run marvellously on the Frame’s own internals, and more complex 3D fare like Dungeons of Eternity or Ghost Town can perform just fine on lowered settings. Simpler stuff, like Cubism or Google’s Tilt Brush, will bother it even less.

The crown jewel of the Frame’s standalone library, however, is Half-Life: Alyx. True, it’s seven years old now, but the erstwhile Index killer app was never originally designed to run on anything other than chunky PCs. The version that runs directly on the Frame is therefore a newly redeveloped build, native to the ARM-based processor, and it’s an impressive yardstick for what the headset can do without streaming help. Cuts are mainly limited to rendering rez and the visual smoothness of animations, leaving the original’s impeccable world detailing and breadth of interactivity untouched.

If standalone VR play has a weakness, it’s not performance but battery life. On default settings, including an automatic refresh rate drop from 120Hz to 72Hz, I only got 1h 03m out of my fully-charged Frame when playing Alyx on it. It’s more like two hours on pure PC streaming, which still isn’t outstanding, though to be frank I’m too partial to face-breathing breaks to play VR for that long anyway.

The third and, perhaps, most pioneering facet of the Frame’s games-playing power is how it runs flat/non-VR games in a virtual theatre view. Not that this is conceptually original, as VR headsets have been doing it for years, but then that’s always been over streaming; through techniques both sensible and extravagant, Valve have made the Frame the first of its ilk to run flat games from your existing Steam library in standalone mode.

The redesigned, more naturally game-agnostic controllers help with this, as does the use of SteamOS as an operating system, which effectively unifies your VR and non-VR collections on the headset itself. But, since not every developer has the resources to make ARM-native versions of the x86-intended games, the biggest deal here is FEX, a newly-added SteamOS component.

Like Proton, which has made thousands of Windows games playable on the Linux-based Steam Machine and Deck, FEX – which Valve has been funding the development of for years – is a compatibility layer. It works to help software designed for chips based on the x86 architecture, like the Intel and AMD CPUs in our desktops, play nice with chips of the rival ARM achitecture. The result, put simply, is that the Frame gets all the low-profile, low-power advantages of ARM hardware with far, far fewer of the games compatibility problems, which would still exist on something like a Quest 3 even if you were to get a Windows emulator running on it.

Or, to put it even simpler: you can play Hollow Knight: Silksong on the sofa, with an effectively cinema-sized screen, and controllers that have more than two buttons apiece.

And that is very cool, at first. The more I took advantage of FEX, though, the more I wondered if its most exciting applications lay elsewhere. Alas, flat game compatibility still feels quite narrow on the Frame, even if it’s performance rather than CPU architecture that’s to blame. As adequately as Alyx runs, ultimately this Snapdragon processor has even less horsepower than that of an original Steam Deck – so while very simple games like Silksong, Signalis, and Hades 2 run fine, even less demanding 3D games can be a toss up. Big Walk is playable on Medium settings, but Wheel World’s lowest visuals can barely scrape 30fps in places where the Deck would have it hitting 60fps. Vholume, whose minimum specs list 4GB of RAM and a lowly GeForce GTX 960, struggles to get above 20fps.

I’m also not entirely convinced of its use cases. The giant-screen effect of a VR theatre is, to my understanding, often enjoyed by those without space for a honking great monitor or TV at home – which is valid. Though the focus on standalone support suggests Valve also have portability in mind, and the Frame is more cumbersome, less powerful, shorter-lasting, and more expensive than a Steam Deck OLED.

Nonetheless, in driving the creation of FEX, the Frame could well have established a legacy that stretches far beyond the plastic confines of a single VR headset. ARM chips are, right now, found in millions of devices – laptops, tablets, phones – and even Nvidia are going with ARM architecture for their first foray into combined CPU/GPU SoCs. These aren’t entirely incapable of becoming makeshift gaming PCs, but it’s still an awful lot of computers that could, in theory, be used to play an awful lot more games with FEX’s help. And more people playing more often has never been a bad thing.

As for the Steam Frame itself, it’s clearly a headset full of ideas. Some of these work better than others, but then even if you mentally slice off the flat-playing stuff and consider it purely as a VR device, it’s still pulling tricks and making improvements that no other headset has thought to do. Certainly that none have actually achieved.

These, importantly, include remedies for VR pain points that have existed for ages. Unreliable wireless connections: fixed. Tricky setups: simplified. Weird controllers: normalised. Needing a Meta account: not needing a Meta account. When the Frame can do this much, this well, I’m practically forced at inside-out sensorpoint to conclude that if I was buying a VR kit for myself, it’d be this one.

I don’t think taking that stance that means making excuses for just how expensive the Frame is; the 1TB version I tested is £1,089 / $1,299, almost double the UK price of a top-spec Quest 3. Having also used the Ergonomic Accessories Kit, I’d say too that the enhanced hand straps are essential enough – particularly for handsy shooters like Alyx – that you’d need to seriously consider factoring in a £59 / $59 set as well. The Frame is the best there is, but good lord, does it make you pay for it.

title: Shetland’s Most Wanted
author: Carolyn Wells
content:
Daniel Shailer embeds with the tiny separatist group “Shetland First,” whose members believe the Shetland Islands were never legitimately ceded to Scotland. Its 83‑year‑old leader, Stuart Hill—shipwreck survivor, serial litigant, self‑proclaimed weather‑controller—is such a compelling eccentric that Shailer ends up as absorbed in Hill’s own story as in the broader currents of populism on these remote isles.

Previously, Hill has focused on relatively esoteric points of history and legalese. Now, on the advice of his chief campaign advisor, ChatGPT, he is meeting people where they are: should council tax go up while official salaries get bumped? Is it fair to live in fuel poverty at the footsteps of Britain’s largest onshore wind farm?

‘There are all these injustices, and once you read the history, you can see a basic injustice,’ Hill says. ‘Everybody seems to be kind of comfortable with it, but at the same time there’s a basic undercurrent of dissatisfaction.’

title: Paid Phones
author: Seyward Darby
content:
The most recent winner of the National Magazine Award for feature writing describes his turn to payday lending apps when AI gobbled up his livelihood (aka penning promotional web content for business clients). Sharp and darkly funny, the essay chronicles yet another nail in the coffin of the American dream:

Albert founder Yinon Ravid has said that he chose his app’s name for its suggestion of the kind of “smart, unassuming friend” you might come to for financial advice, but today, when I hear the name Albert, I am far more likely to picture an overwhelming force bent on my total destruction, a figure you might spot while being burned alive in a dream—black-robed, pale, teeth bared. When I first joined the app, about eighteen months ago, Albert offered me $25.00. To acquire this loan, I was required to pay an additional fee: A $6.99 instant deposit charge plus the cost of a $19.99-per-month subscription to Albert’s Standard plan, due in one week’s time alongside the full loan repayment. (If I really wanted to make the most of my $25.00, I also had the option of Albert’s $39.99-per-month Genius plan, which, among a very small handful of other talents, can “find restaurants based on your location, or in a specific area.”) On its own, this might’ve been manageable, but, true to the CRL’s findings, Albert’s offerings alone couldn’t keep me afloat, and so I soon signed up for the rest of the payday apps, each one toting its share of instant deposit and subscription fees. (Gallingly, Dave—the only publicly traded company of the bunch, valued at $4.72 billion as of this writing—has the nerve to ask for a tip after each transaction, a move that I suspect even the flintiest strip mall grift artists would dismiss as gauche.)
