title: Why Western democracy is ailing and how to fix it | Aeon Essays
content:
If the people around you are spiteful and callous and will not hear you, fall down before them and beg their forgiveness; for in truth you are to blame for their not wanting to hear you.– from The Brothers Karamazov (1880) by Fyodor Dostoevsky

If Western democracies were companies, they would be dismissed as lifestyle businesses whose managers (ie, political leaders) run them to promote their own interests and wealth. Leaders pursue projects that benefit the few, rather than national goals, and leave their countries with low economic growth, heavy debt and rampant white-collar crime. We entered this era of an unjust social order, political malaise and destabilisation almost half a century ago when the US president Ronald Reagan and the UK prime minister Margaret Thatcher introduced libertarian reforms that were embraced globally.

At his first cabinet meeting as president in 1981, Reagan distributed copies of Mandate for Leadership, whose 3,000 pages came out of the Heritage Foundation, a conservative research group in Washington, DC. This became the ideology of neoliberalism, which advocated a smaller state, industry deregulation, tax cuts, strengthened defence, and roll-back of social engineering. A year later, 60 per cent of the Mandate’s proposals had been adopted by the Reagan administration, and The New York Times called it ‘the manifesto of the Reagan revolution’. His initiative engaged Thatcher, and spread globally to dominate public policy in democracies around the world.

My perspective is that of an engineer with a career as a corporate strategist and, more recently, finance academic. In 2000, shortly after the Y2K scare, I left the corporate world for academia and research into decision-making by international finance organisations. In a round of industrial tourism, I interviewed more than 50 finance executives in Istanbul, London, Melbourne and New York. This led to three books, including Applied Investment Theory (2016), which criticised the justice system’s failure to prosecute corruption and criminal activity in large companies and among elected officials.

A framework used in corporate finance to explain the behaviour of organisations and individuals is the structure-conduct-performance (SCP) model, and it can help us understand the effects of the changes that Reagan and Thatcher brought to Western democracies. SCP conceptualises decisions within a multidimensional framework; when applied to countries, this framework postulates that their conditions are driven by the structure of institutions, laws and conventions; which drives the conduct or decisions of government, individuals and organisations; and that in turn leads to performance or outcomes.

Reagan and Thatcher asserted that unleashing markets and shrinking the state would ensure prosperity. Their signature initiatives of industry deregulation, tax reduction, market liberalisation and labour market reform won the day.

It did not take long, however, for the trickle-down effects of tax cuts funded by government debt to prove disastrous. Most obvious was the Black Monday stock market crash of October 1987. Neoliberalism had reduced the capacity of public institutions to manage systemic risks, and – as the authority and ability of government to regulate industry shrank – moral hazard spiked.

Infrastructure is a simple way to illustrate the realignment between state, markets and democratic institutions over the past half-century. Following the Second World War, Western governments invested heavily in transportation networks, energy systems and other public capital. Privatisation and deregulation reversed this trend, with cutbacks to public works projects: when roads and bridges, water systems and so on aged, productivity faltered.

Promises of prosperity by Reagan, Thatcher and other advocates of neoliberalism were mistaken because it brought only fragility to previously prosperous democracies. From an SCP perspective, the trickle-down of market liberalisation and financialisation brought slowing growth, rising debt burdens, institutional weakness, and declining public trust.

Some basic facts help to understand these claims, and give a sense of the impacts of neoliberal policies. Consider financial data since 1980 for the rich liberal democracies among the members of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Reduced tax revenue forced governments to rely on borrowings, and government debt – as shown in the left-hand graph of Figure 1 below – surged from 40 to 65 per cent as a share of GDP. Meanwhile, government expenditure kept pace with the economy at almost half of GDP.

In the right-hand chart of Figure 1 below, we see the economic consequences of high, unfunded government debt. The blue line tracks growth of GDP per capita, which gradually slowed from nearly 3 per cent annually in the 1980s to barely 1 per cent today. At the same time, deregulated credit markets encouraged households to borrow, and their debt more than doubled as a proportion of GDP. Quite obviously, neoliberalism did not deliver on its promises of economic growth and increased personal wealth.

The big winner from 50 years of neoliberal policy has been the finance sector. As government and household debt surged out of control, global capital became ever freer, bankers’ propensity for risk surged, and speculative activity flourished. Financial institutions grew dramatically in size and influence. In the US and the UK, financial institutions have become a power in terms of profits and political influence. But, as shown in Figure 2 below, they set up a roughly seven-year cycle of market bubbles followed by crash and recession, which created super, unearned wealth for investor elites. Meanwhile, the middle class and below saw home ownership and comfortable retirement drift out of reach, especially for Gen Y.

Probably the most powerful impact of neoliberalism has been on governance. Weakened corporate governance led to spectacular bankruptcies, with equally poor government strategy such as the failure to find promised weapons of mass destruction in Iraq, the 2008-09 global financial crisis, and over-the-top COVID-19 lockdowns. These generated anger and frustration that still linger, as indicated in Figure 3 above, where the rising global uncertainty index gives a rough but illuminating perspective on popular political sentiments.

The decline in the economic stability and health of Western political democracies over the past 40 years is not simply a run of bad luck, because it did not occur in countries such as China and India that resisted its blandishments. Bad decisions that inflicted sweeping damage to democracies came from deliberate structural misalignments between democratic institutions and social and economic realities.

Rectifying the malaise in Western political democracies requires realignment of the political paradigm, starting with support for decision-makers who can foster improved institutions and practices.

Though it may seem counterintuitive, we must raise the pay of top government officials. Consider the annual base salaries for heads of government of OECD member countries: around half fall in the range US$150,000-400,000; only Switzerland and Australia are higher, and the rest are even lower. The base salary of the US president has been fixed at $400,000 since 2001, while the UK prime minister’s salary of around £170,000 (cUS$230,000) is less today than that paid to Gordon Brown in 2009.

While money is not the only driver of occupational choice, underpayment invites mediocrity and the entitled, and encourages corruption. Political salaries need to be competitive. Leaders of government should be remunerated by reference to the compensation of CEOs of major domestic companies, with the pay of other politicians and senior government officials brought into line. In a mid-ranking country like Australia, trebling the base salary of members of the national parliament from a piddling US$170,000 per year would cost less than $80 million. That’s a cheap price for sound management of a $2 trillion economy.

Better-paid and better-financed candidates will help shake up the political duopoly

Voters paying their politicians more will expect better candidates and deeper competition. Their choices will be enhanced by more complete disclosure of candidates’ assets and interests, as required for candidates in India. Media denigration of politicians’ personal lives is an obvious deterrent to meritorious candidates. Australia has faced this, and allows individuals to sue for serious invasions of privacy when information relating to them has been misused.

The cost of election campaigns is another major impediment, especially to candidates from outside the establishment. Emerging candidates and parties would be helped by democracy vouchers as introduced in Seattle city elections, which are distributed to voters during election campaigns for them to support preferred parties or candidates.

Many democracies run longstanding two-party political systems: Liberal and Labor in Australia, Labour and Conservative in the UK, Republican and Democrat in the US. Even though parties swap government after every election or two, they co-ordinate through continual exchange of ideas. This duopoly structure stymies new directions and substantive reform (Noam Chomsky’s observation that ‘the smart way to keep people passive and obedient is to strictly limit the spectrum of acceptable opinion, but allow very lively debate within that spectrum’ comes to mind). Better-paid and better-financed candidates will help shake up the political duopoly and more closely review democracies’ performance.

Many politicians have a growth-first agenda. The Florida governor Ron DeSantis, for example, told his electorate: ‘We need a new generation of leaders who will promote policies that will foster economic growth.’ This imperative is important in light of the management truism that ‘what gets measured gets managed’, even when it’s pointless.

The most common measure of democracies’ performance is gross domestic product (GDP), which is a dumb yardstick because it simply records the value of goods and services that have a price. We get no information about their social or political meaning; nor details of other activities. As a result, unhealthy citizens, expenditure on wars, and rebuilding after accidents and disasters can all increase GDP. It does not count any value from the productivity and other benefits of free services such as the internet and AI (beyond their development and any subscription costs); nor does it count natural resources, unpaid labour or improvements in quality.

GDP growth at all costs encourages poor policy. Business corporations with a ‘triple bottom line’ such as profit, people and the planet better recognise social ideals than GDP. One country that acknowledges this is New Zealand whose Living Standards Framework measures the wellbeing of individuals and institutions as well as the country’s wealth. Such balanced measures should be a minimum standard for all governments.

Voters increasingly resent the burgeoning global oligarchy of the most wealthy and best-connected. Thus a survey across OECD countries in 2023 found that seven in 10 respondents want a more equal distribution of economic resources, and half think that disparities in political power are too high.

This concentration of wealth encourages oligarchs to protect their interests at the general community’s expense

Hard data back up these concerns. As shown in the left-hand graph of Figure 4 below, in large democracies, the share of total wealth held by the richest 1 per cent fell to its lowest levels around the mid-1980s. But it has rebounded since then: that 1 per cent now holds more than a quarter of total wealth in France, Germany and the US, and more than 20 per cent of the wealth in Australia, Italy and the UK.

This concentration of wealth encourages oligarchs to protect their interests at the general community’s expense. Most obviously, they introduced big money into politics, as evidenced by a US study in 2025, which found that 30-45 per cent of private contributions to presidential candidates come from the wealthiest 1 per cent of voters. Oligarchs have frozen out citizens and structured ‘cartel parties’ that use state resources for themselves.

Government economic policy is now a major source of oligarchs’ income. According to the management consultants McKinsey, higher government debt and easier credit increase financial assets in the private sector and promote asset price inflation. This disproportionately rewards wealthier households because they derive more of their income from financial, rather than labour, earnings. Similar benefit comes from corporate welfare, free markets and deregulation.

The benefit of increased government debt to wealthy households is confirmed in the right-hand chart of Figure 4 above. Since 1980, government debt in Western democracies almost doubled its share of GDP, while the proportion of wealth held by the top 1 per cent jumped by a quarter.

The risk from oligarchs’ power was summed up neatly by the futurist Aldo Grech: ‘Politics has been shaped through money and access’ and ‘a very small minority has steadily rewritten the rules that govern economics, labour, housing, healthcare, media, and even attention itself.’ The solution is to more closely tie wealth to its producer to limit its lifetime and stymie entrenchment of a hereditary ruling class. This would come from throttling excessive inter-generational transfers through a progressive death tax.

Many countries share the US experience that nothing seems to deter corporate fraud, systemic gambles and political misconduct. Congressional inquiries were all that confronted Enron and WorldCom, Wall Street and the financial crisis, Volkswagen’s emissions-test manipulation, big tech antitrust bills, and the opioid crisis. The US senator Elizabeth Warren expressed widespread frustration at ineffective control of such white-collar crimes when she pointed to blatant fraud during the financial crisis of 2008 and complained that ‘not one major bank executive was even charged, much less prosecuted and taken to trial.’ Two impediments are obvious.

First is the reigning medieval legal principle of mens rea (Latin for ‘guilty mind’) which makes conviction for crime contingent on proof of intent so as to distinguish criminal acts from accident or negligence. Intent is obvious with crimes against person and property, but it’s very difficult to prove with white-collar crimes such as fraud and market manipulations.

Strict liability should be extended to cover the fraud tolerated in many industries

A second impediment to prosecution of white-collar crime is the artificial separation between responsibility for regulatory breaches and criminal offences. As examples, workplace fatalities are investigated in most countries within a department of labour or similar; and financial fraud and misreporting are investigated by securities regulators. But regulators lack investigative expertise, can become too close to their industry, and can lack independence, as evidenced by the revolving door between them and the corporations they are supposed to be regulating.

The principle of mens rea and the bureaucratic investigation of white-collar crime protect well-connected criminals. Securing accountability requires the introduction of strict liability where individuals and relevant company officers become legally responsible for criminal and regulatory breaches. This already applies to most traffic, product liability and environmental offences, and last year the UK introduced a new strict liability corporate criminal offence of failure to prevent fraud. Strict liability should be extended to cover the fraud tolerated in many industries, and penalise criminal incompetence as evidenced by bankruptcy, workplace fatalities and the sale of faulty products. Defence would be confined to a reasonable belief that the action was legal, and intent is relevant only when determining the sentence.

Regulatory breaches and white-collar criminal offences should both be investigated by a common police force, independent of the crime and perpetrators. The best example is Singapore, whose police force has a Commercial Affairs Department that investigates a wide range of financial and corporate offences, including fraud, market misconduct and company law breaches.

Let us close with the oft-neglected ‘how’ of political transformation. In 1962, Thomas Kuhn wrote the book on its preconditions. The most relevant is accepting that the existing paradigm is ineffective, which is clear from voter dissatisfaction and loss of faith in leaders of the major democracies. As evidence, in elections held in 2024, voters around the world swung against the incumbent government in every developed country that held elections.

The times also favour structural political reform. In their review of the many elections of 2024, the Stockholm-based International Institute for Democracy identified ‘a profound and growing … sense that we are at a historical juncture where we must revisit and reassess the strength of our democratic culture and institutions.’ Moreover, today’s conditions resemble those of the dynamic Roaring 1920s, which also began after a shock pandemic, saw rapid introduction of new consumer technologies (cars, the telephone, movies, airplanes), cultural dynamism (jazz, Art Deco, Surrealism, psychoanalysis), as well as strong growth in economies and financial markets. The decade ended in the crash of 1929 and the Great Depression, but they were followed by sweeping political reform (Keynesian fiscal policy, adult suffrage, consolidation of political parties, and voter-driven initiatives).

There is no shortage of ideas to reform our democracies. Because voters acting as democratic troops in peaceful demonstration of mass dissatisfaction will always command attention, street protests involving at least 3.5 per cent of the population are almost guaranteed success. Other successful tactics include confrontational protests such as boycotts of elections, petitions and lobbying.

Tackling the crisis in democracy requires more democracy

Citizens’ assemblies are a promising path to political reform. These are best known in Ireland where 99 members of the public are randomly chosen to represent the country’s demography. They work like a super-jury to consider an issue over some days of meetings, and prepare a report with recommendations. Topics have included abortion, climate change, the challenges and opportunities of an ageing population, and drugs use.

Even these modest proposals threaten entrenched politicians and their parties, oligarchs and corporations. Opponents are so powerful and organised that reforming the democratic system inevitably requires securing insider support.

By the 20th century, Western democracies defeated the brutalities of material scarcity and political oppression. Today’s citizens are orders of magnitude better off than their ancestors in terms of income, technologies, health, and knowledge. Even so, aspects of basic wellbeing – such as rising income and affordable, quality housing – are receding for many. Performance has also been poor on non-economic measures such as public health, environmental quality, trust in science, and infrastructure reliability.

So, what happened? Recalling our structure-conduct-performance model, the short answer is that neoliberal reforms beginning in the 1980s weakened the institutions on which democracy depends. Tackling the crisis in democracy requires more democracy that breaks the monopoly position of ineffective incumbents and conservative duopolies. This comes through incentivising better-quality election candidates and alternative parties, modernising institutions, and rebalancing economic power.

title: It’s not just screen time: kids are bombarded by hectic media | Aeon Essays
content:
I am at the airport gate waiting to depart, watching passengers hurry past with rolling suitcases and paper cups of coffee. A small boy sits very still beside his mother. He holds an iPad close to his chest, almost in a cramp, clutching the screen as if it might otherwise run away. I hear loud clapping hands and squeaking children’s voices. I lean over and see a cartoon character in green snatch a toy from another character in pink. The pink character begins to cry, tears splashing from enormous eyes like sprinkles. The green character shouts sorry. Instantly, the tears stop and a wide smile replaces the tears before I have blinked. And, before I have even worked out whether the characters are speaking English or Arabic (as the mother does to the boy), the scene has changed and the two characters are rowing a boat with a random song in the background. The boy’s eyes dart on the screen from right to left, centre, down. His body is still but his attention is being hurried from cue to cue.

This is the problem I have come to think of as the pace of children’s media.

Children’s media are usually judged by their content and quantity: how many minutes watched and whether it was educational, age-appropriate, diverse, prosocial, commercial or safe. These questions matter and, with my colleagues, I have studied them through experiments and contributed to guidelines, regulations, or toolkits for designers. But we have been missing a bigger design feature that may be just as consequential: the time a medium gives a child to make meaning. A programme or app can contain good lessons and still move too quickly for those lessons to settle. For instance, in the US animated educational series Ask the StoryBots (2016-20), the subject matter may be genuinely rich – why the sky is blue, how eyes work, or where planets come from – but the explanation unfolds through rapid jokes, songs, visual shifts and sudden changes in style. Before a child has time to sit with one image or idea, the scene has moved on to the next, with a burst of information.

Different media have different temporal demands: a digital picture book, a game, a television episode and an app each ask a child to attend differently. But, across media, the important question is whether the pace suits the experience that the narrative claims to support. Does it give children time to follow a story, grasp a concept, identify with a character, regulate emotion or share attention with another person? Or does it continually hurry them toward the next cue, the next reward, the next burst of stimulation?

When media move too quickly, the layers of experience collapse into one another. A child may laugh at someone slipping on a banana peel but imitate only the visible silliness, missing the anticipation and reversal that make the joke work. A character may comfort a friend, but if the scene moves on too quickly, the child has little time to recognise the repair, or imagine doing the same in the kindergarten room. To develop empathy in the early years, a child must notice that another person feels something different. That small act of crossing over takes time.

In this sense, pace is not a minor stylistic feature of children’s media. It is one of the ways media imagine the child. Is the child a consumer to be retained, a nervous system to be stimulated, a vessel to be filled with educational content – or a person whose attention is still forming, and who therefore needs time to arrive?

People who worry about children and screens tend to worry about violent content, advertising, or whether a phonics app calling itself ‘educational’ truly supports phonics. These are reasonable worries and I share them. But spend five minutes watching what many young children watch, and you will see how fast, loud and bright everything on the screen has become. It does not matter whether the child is watching on a smartphone in the car or on a television at home. The screen has inherited the adult logic of media design.

That logic is, for the most part, the logic of the attention economy. It overwhelms and overshouts, making it easier for the screen to steer the viewer. The attention economy has introduced a host of small design features for shortening time. The Like button is faster than writing an appreciative comment. A progress bar tells us how many minutes remain in an article before we have decided whether to read to the end. Increasingly, AI appears beside long documents with an offer that sounds helpful but carries a philosophy: this text is long; would you like a quick summary?

The child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other

There are, of course, features that work in the opposite direction. The delayed message and the pop-up that asks: ‘Are you sure you want to delete this?’ are two examples. Such features interrupt automatic action and return a fragment of judgment to the user. A nature documentary with linearity and the interpretive presence of an adult voice is a great model for children’s media; for example, in the TV show Prehistoric Planet (2022-25), David Attenborough’s voiceover and the camera’s zoom-ins encourage children to look closely and wonder about unfamiliar life. But these are exceptions within a larger system in which speed is treated as the default.

When learning is crowded with content that keeps jumping ahead – a crisis appears, a mission begins, a spaceship launches, a door opens – the child’s attention is restarted as each problem is introduced and immediately solved. Such media may gesture at teamwork or perseverance, but the speed of the format leaves little time for those lessons to sink in. In the animated TV series Paw Patrol (2013-), for instance, a rescue is clear and reassuring: someone is in trouble, pups assemble, each uses a skill, and order is restored. Yet the movement from problem to rescue to resolution is often so efficient that the child is swept along by urgency rather than invited to dwell on responsibility or care for the other. Similarly, in the app-based game Hot Wheels Unlimited, building tracks and racing cars may suggest creativity and problem-solving, but the dominant rhythm is acceleration: boost, race, crash, win, unlock, repeat.

Research has told us many useful things about children’s media. We know that some educational television (like Sesame Street) can support learning. We know that some apps are better designed than others. We know that interactive features in digital books can help when they serve the story, and distract when they do not. We know that characters and narratives shape children’s ideas about identity, gender and social life. Pace cuts across all of these questions as the condition under which content becomes experience.

Screen time can run fast or slow. This is partly why merely clocking ‘screen time’ is too crude a measure. Two children may each watch 20 minutes of media and have entirely different encounters with time. In one case, the child is moved through a coherent story with pauses, repetitions and recognisable emotional beats. In another, she is pulled through 10 clips, 30 characters, flashing colours, sudden songs and rewards that arrive before thought has had time to form. The clock records the same duration but the child does not live the same time.

And parents are rightly worried: a four-year-old does not come to media with adult reserves of self-regulation. She is still learning how to stay with a feeling, how to wait for a story to unfold, how to connect one event to another, how to notice that a character’s sadness matters before the joke wipes it away. If a programme moves too quickly, it may encourage a child to expect information to arrive in rapid, constantly shifting bursts, making slower, more sustained forms of attention harder to tolerate. Stopping this vicious cycle starts by asking what exactly makes children’s media fast or slow.

A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think

Don’t get me wrong, I am not saying that slow is always good or better than fast media. Some lively children’s media can be excellent; some slow media can be dull, inert or badly made. The point is that good children’s media give a child time to complete an act of attention. Bad media keep interrupting that act before it can become a memory or play.

When my research group compared children’s shows, apps and digital stories, we saw that pace can become a set of design choices. A story can move in a way that helps a child anticipate what comes next, or it can jump so quickly between scenes that cause and effect become blurred. A screen can guide the eye toward one important object, or fill the frame with competing movement.

This is why the familiar adult language of ‘engagement’ is so poor for children. A child can look intensely engaged while being given very little time to think. In the Children’s Slow Media Project, we have therefore tried to make these differences visible. We evaluate children’s media by looking at how these media organise time. We ask whether the narrative is coherent enough to follow; whether the sensory field overwhelms meaning-making at specific age junctures; whether the design builds in stopping points, where the story can be digested before it goes on. Does a piece of media allow learning to develop through meaningful repetition? And does a story or piece create openings for a child and adult, or two children, to notice something together?

When in March 2026 the UK Department for Education advised parents of children aged under five to choose ‘slow-paced, age-appropriate’ content, without saying what slow-paced actually is, our group sought to make the term concrete.

What makes a show slow or fast for a given child? It depends. Children differ by age, temperament, language, sensory sensitivity and circumstance; thus, without testing their responses, it is impossible to provide a firm recommendation: a show that suits one four-year-old may overwhelm another. We therefore give ratings only to provide a map for adult judgment. The ratings are illustrations, inviting parents to check whether their child is being given enough time to complete an act of attention.

The shows scoring highest on the slow rubric are those that leave room around the characters’ actions and allow the child to recognise the actions. Often there is a face, a puppet, a song, a greeting, a familiar body on screen that treats attention as a relationship. Indeed, the power of programmes such as the US show Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood (1968-2001), the Norwegian series Fantorangen (2007-), and the British shows In the Night Garden… (2007-09) and Teletubbies (1997-2001) lies in their ability to build a rapport with the child and then repeat, almost as in a ritual. Here, small acts and greetings or songs provide a familiar frame, almost like a safety net, within which new concepts can be introduced. In the Australian animated series Bluey (2018-24), play often begins in an ordinary family situation and develops into imaginative games that involve parents, siblings and friends; the pace can be lively, but it tends to return the child to pretend play, negotiation and emotional understanding. In the animated TV series The Adventures of Paddington (2019-25) – a British-French co-production – gentle mishaps are usually held inside a world of curiosity, politeness, family and repair, so comedy becomes a route into perseverance or social understanding. Such programmes are slow because they leave openings through which the story can travel back into meaning and play.

The child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat

Conversations between characters are another way in which higher-ranked shows convey new concepts with appropriate pace. When introduced with context, a new word or idea might not be immediately clear, but the child can notice and infer. Over time, the child arrives at understanding, and this slow, even arduous process helps the concept stick. For example, in one episode of Daniel Tiger’s Neighbourhood (2012-) – based on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood – Daniel is nervous about trying the swing. The scene allows that feeling to be acknowledged, sung through, and gradually transformed into confidence, with support from Daniel’s friend Jodi and her grandmother. Similarly, in the Sesame Street-based game app Elmo Loves ABCs, a letter is traced, sounded, repeated, connected to words, and encountered through touch and play.

The lowest-scoring media are those in which the child’s attention is kept in motion by a manipulative rhythm that continuously restarts attention with the next tune, next bright image, next comic beat, next loop of familiarity or personalised nudge. Instead of allowing the child to settle into the story, such children’s shows repeatedly pull attention back; the same is true of many preschool game apps built around loops of reward and progression.

Evaluating children’s popular media taught me that pace is a revealing measure of quality but also a proxy for a deeper question about the child’s agency, their own sense of self.

The real distinction is whether a medium leaves room for the child’s own attention or continually redirects it. When every pause is filled, every uncertainty immediately resolved and every wandering thought pulled back by a brighter cue, waiting and reflection can begin to feel intolerable. The child learns to reach for the next stimulus before the previous one has had time to settle. To give space for a child’s attention to drift inward, to reflect, is therefore to leave room for the child’s inner life. Slow media changes the relation between screen and child by saying: you may arrive at your own pace.

Some critics may dismiss slow media as nostalgia: a longing for the children’s television of the previous generation, or a privilege available only to parents with time and large bookshelves and big houses with quiet rooms. But that is a notion we should refuse. The attention economy has trained us to treat a child’s pause as a problem, a wandering gaze as lost engagement, and an unfilled moment as wasted time. The opposite is true – slow time gives children the space to perceive, process, respond and make meaning – and it can be designed for in children’s media.

Like energy drinks, fast media promise more capacity than the child actually has: more attention is supposed to lead to better performance. Fast media feel like an extension of the child’s energy, but the bargain is unsustainable and unhealthy. What looks like support can become dependency, and what promises engagement and learning is actually compulsion.

Children need media that do not merely occupy them, instruct them or keep them quiet. They benefit and grow from stories and shows that preserve children’s capacity for inwardness and their relation to others. In fast media, the child’s attention is continually propped up by the next stimulus. Slow media insist on the opposite. In the end, the aim is not to withdraw children from the digital world, but to make that world more worthy of them.

title: What palmistry and medicine have always had in common | Aeon Essays
content:
Signs of the future are marked in our hands, or so any palmist will declare. But do hands also hold signs of the past? Do they have a history? Over decades of research as a historian of medicine and of human bodies, I’d never imagined such a niche question. And then it was sparked in an instant, between one second and the next, in the time it takes to open a manila folder. For another project altogether I was in the UK to research the papers of Charlotte Wolff, a physician trained in Berlin in the 1920s and living in London in the late 1930s, a Jewish refugee. Opening a file labelled ‘Zoo, 1938’, I came across a massive, delicate palm print: it belonged to Mok, a lowland gorilla at London Zoo. Two days after Mok’s death, the keeper had granted Wolff special permission to enter the morgue and collect a pattern that had been too dangerous to acquire in life.

Mok’s palm print was both forceful and touching. Indeed, I was tempted to literally touch, to hold hands across time, across species, and across the worlds of the living and the dead. The emotive power was unmistakeable, yet for all my training as a historian, it was inscrutable to me. I was also puzzled why Wolff, an exceptionally clever physician, seemed to be practising palm-reading, which today is associated with magic and the occult. Could there be such a thing as medical palmistry?

Over time, I learned that the answer is a clear, but unlikely, ‘yes’. Wolff was looking for the so-called ‘simian line’, a particular crease that some humans share with other primate species. Long ago, in embryonic time, the patterns on each of our tiny, clenched palms were formed. For most of us, three main lines were created. For some of us – up to 5 per cent – the so-called head and heart lines fused into a single crease stretching across the palm from one side to the other. Robert De Niro, Hillary Clinton and Benedict Cumberbatch each boast a simian line on their palms. Tony Blair apparently does on both hands, an even rarer distinction. In the 1920s, the London physician Francis Crookshank delighted in announcing that even the Virgin Mary had a simian line, directing people to see for themselves in Renaissance devotional art.

To this day, midwives still quickly check neonatal palms, not because the newborn might be divinely conceived, but because a single crease has a high incidence in those of us with a particular chromosomal anomaly known as trisomy 21. Not everyone with this transverse crease has Down’s syndrome. And not everyone with Down’s syndrome has the so-called (still-called) simian crease. And yet, so strong is the correlation that this sign on the hand was a key element of clinical diagnosis until recently. It is fair, if strange, to say that the history of palmistry is the history of medicine.

As a rule, physicians relish the weird in their own medical history, but I’ve learned that they don’t appreciate this particular claim. Yet, in turning their backs on the medical history of palmistry, they turn their backs on some towering figures.

In the summer of 1663 in Cambridge, young Isaac Newton walked over to the fair on Stourbridge Common and bought himself a new book, Palmistry, the Secrets Thereof Disclosed. It was written by a physician, who instructed that the lines, angles, shapes and hatches on the palm needed to be read strictly and precisely with a measuring compass. Here was a geometry of the hand that needed to be decoded mathematically. No wonder Newton was interested. Yet we also know that Newton attended to ‘occult’ knowledge that purported to be previously unknown or hidden, hence ‘secrets disclosed’. (In fact, physicians still use the word in that plain way: ‘occult pain’, for example, is of unknown or unseen origin.)

Newton was exercised by the learned traditions kept in ancient manuscripts and precious early printed books in Arabic, in Hebrew and in Latin, later circulating in vernaculars across Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. He was especially consumed by hermetic natural magic and the mysticism of ancient Jewish Kabbalah that had been Christianised in the Renaissance. This included what was then called ‘chiromancy’, discerning character, health and fortunes from the hand, from the Greek cheir. Medieval and early modern ‘prognostication’ – divining the future – was slowly turning into medical prognostics.

Most early chiromantic texts were written by physicians. From Paracelsus to the Paracelsian physician Robert Fludd, Newton had them all in his library. Sometimes the simian line was clearly illustrated, yet this particular sign had not yet been analysed by the comparative anatomists, the biostatisticians or the primatologists who would later name it.

Both folk palmistry and learned chiromancy were reference points for a modern anatomy of the hand

The hand has a history of natural magic and occult knowledges, but it is also just anatomy, and so it appears in a plainer anatomical canon too. Yet that tradition is enchanted in its own way. One of the 19th century’s most eminent anatomists, Charles Bell, wrote The Hand (1833), a medical text on God’s design. And not long after, humanity’s deep past was being re-told through the human hand. In The Descent of Man (1871), Charles Darwin recounted that, one day, standing upright, the hand of the primate called Homo sapiens was free to grasp and so to evolve differently, uniquely. It is no coincidence that it was in the 1860s that the term ‘haptic’ arose, from the Greek haptikós, not just to touch, but to grasp or perceive. The hand of this new species of primate was set free for matters beyond locomotion, ultimately giving humankind ‘universal dominion’ over all other creatures, as Darwin wrote, quoting Bell. What a revolutionary idea! Friedrich Engels certainly thought so, as he wrangled the human hand into his dialectics of nature, his search for the material drivers of history. Bell’s anatomical textbook had shown the human hand grasping that all-important tool.

Both folk palmistry and learned chiromancy were reference points for a modern anatomy of the hand. In the 1820s, the Czech anatomist Jan Evangelista Purkinje – known for his fingerprint studies – also analysed the crease patterns on human as well as monkey palms, specifying new terms: the lines of opposition, abduction, adduction, extension, and flexion. Yet, in order to clarify, he had to explain these as the life line, the line of Mars, the line of matrimony, the table line, the line of Venus, the line of Rascetta, and the lines of honour and fortune. Traditional palmistry, in other words, was his anatomical reference point. Nearly a century later, when a then-obscure English doctor named Reginald Langdon Down admitted a patient to the family’s private asylum, he recorded ‘Hands, no head line’ in the admission files. Palmists’ terms were his clinical referents too. That was in 1907, just after his own beloved son was born with the syndrome that was yet to be named for his family.

In France, the anatomist Paul Broca had for some time researched palm creases comparatively across humans and other primates, identifying ‘la disposition simienne du pli palmaire’. Over time, le seul pli – the single fold – was the term used in French scholarship, while German anatomists and clinicians referred to vierfingerfurche, the four-finger crease. In English and American studies ‘the simian line’ proved to be an enduring designation. In 1924, an anatomist employed by the London Zoological Society showed clearly that the orangutan had this single transverse line, and sometimes even two in parallel, both running right across the palm.

This was all on Wolff’s mind when she entered the morgue at London Zoo in 1938. Indeed, she had for some time been climbing into the primate cages taking the prints of every live simian she safely could: those of lemurs, spider monkeys, baboons, chimpanzees, orangutans and more. She even took the delicate prints of a hedgehog. Of more stature, perhaps, were the palms of human primates she collected and then interpreted. These were not any old Homo sapiens but very special specimens indeed. As I opened more manila folders in the Wellcome Collection, London, there were the intimate hand-portraits of every interwar cultural luminary imaginable: Aldous Huxley, Virginia Woolf, Vaslav Nijinsky, Maurice Ravel and so many more. Yet the most haunting remained Mok, the dead lowland gorilla.

It’s a delicate history to tell, this comparative anatomy across primate palms that gave rise to the offensive term ‘simian line’. Yet, before we object, sneer, mock, judge or even just enjoy this as the quirky business of early misguided medicine, or worse dismiss it as ‘pseudoscience’, we should note that this is not only an antique history. It tracks right up to our own present, involving some of the most distinguished researchers of the 20th century, Newton’s worthy intellectual descendants.

Around the same time that Wolff was taking Mok’s palm print, in another part of London the medical geneticist Lionel Penrose was beginning a lifetime assessing human palms and finger patterns. He was doing so both geometrically and statistically in a manner more sophisticated than, but not unlike, Francis Galton’s late-19th-century work on fingerprints. It is little known that Galton – often called the ‘father of fingerprinting’– took palm prints too, occasionally wondering if his hypothesis on the individuality of the fingerprint was also discernible in palm lines. This was a tradition of medical and genetic hand-reading that came to be called ‘dermatoglyphics’.

As late as 1990, the simian crease was even sought, detected and analysed prenatally, via ultrasound

In this context, it was the fortune of the so-called simian line to become the perfect exemplar of a classic modern biomedical pair, the visible ‘phenotype’ and its hidden twin, the ‘genotype’. The former is an observable physical trait; the latter is that trait’s unique DNA code or sequence. Sorting out the connection between them was a great driver of mid-20th-century genetics. Over the 1930s and ’40s, before the chromosomal cause of Down’s syndrome was known, clever Penrose could work only with the phenotype – the physical expression – and he was able to statistically correlate the simian line with the syndrome. And then, in the late 1950s, a Paris-based team discovered the genotype that was trisomy 21, the additional chromosome. It was a massive breakthrough, the long-invisible genotype (an extra chromosome) was now visible, a match with its long-visible phenotype (the simian line, le seul pli, vierfingerfurche). We might well say that an occult sign had been revealed.

I expected the medical palmistry – so to say – to then dissipate, to become antiquated, yet to my utter surprise it did not. For decades after the extraordinary chromosomal discovery, these world-leading Paris and London-based geneticists continued to exchange letters with diagrams of hand patterns, still drawing those three – and in some humans, just two – main lines on the palm.

In the 1960s, paediatricians added another palm crease of note, dubbing it the ‘Sydney line’, or sometimes ‘the simian-like line’. As late as 1990, the simian crease was even sought, detected and analysed prenatally, via ultrasound. One study showed that, in seven foetuses with this sign, four had no chromosomal anomaly, and three had trisomy 21. And even today, some of the most prestigious research hospitals in the world explain to parents that their neonatal physician may check the newborn palm, still nominating the ‘simian crease’.

We all know that a straight line can be drawn between any two points. But as a medical historian, can I really draw a line from Newton’s book Palmistry, the Secrets Thereof Disclosed to the prenatal detection of the simian line in the Journal of Ultrasound in Medicine? The first was built from knowledge that is far remote from our own comprehension of the human body. That was a world in which it made every sense that the planet Jupiter and the finger of Jupiter would be connected, a ‘sympathetic’ relation between a celestial macrocosm and a bodily microcosm. Yet I’ve come to appreciate that this apparently magical chiromancy is an archaic version of what modern clinicians do all the time and every day. They read bodily signs.

Medical students are routinely taught the distinction between a symptom felt by the patient, and a sign observed and interpreted by the clinician. This sign (a rash, the colour of nails, a black spot, a pattern in the palm) has that meaning (measles, liver disease, melanoma, Down’s syndrome). And so, all physicians are foundationally schooled in the interpretation of somatic signs. They are medical semioticians, whether or not they would put it that way.

All physicians are medical semioticians, professional and trained readers of bodily signs

The surprising thing is that some physicians put it precisely that way. It was initially strange to me that the London physician who observed the simian line on the Virgin Mary’s palm in the 1920s – Francis Crookshank – was also deeply schooled in the complexities of contemporary linguistics. Pondering the meaning of the simian line that some of his professional colleagues, as well as his patients, displayed, Crookshank began to insist that medicine desperately needed a ‘theory of signs’. One winter’s evening in 1926, he lectured on just that to the Royal College of Physicians and couldn’t understand why his medical brethren first rolled their eyes, and then closed their eyes, falling asleep with boredom. The connection he drew between clinical sign-reading and highly abstract semiotics was just too much. In so many ways, he was speaking a different language, and certainly his essay’s publication in the specialist book The Meaning of Meaning (1923) – to be read mainly by philosophers of language and Oxbridge cultural anthropologists – did nothing to persuade his medical colleagues. It may have been ill-delivered and badly pitched, but the fact is this palm-reading physician was theorising not just the simian line, but everyday clinical business: how signs on the human body are observed, named, and then ascribed meaning. He did so, not only, but not least for the simian line.

All physicians are medical semioticians, professional and trained readers of bodily signs. In his 16th-century treatise on chiromancy, Paracelsus claimed that ‘nothing is so secret in a human being that it does not have an outward sign’. Indeed, a whole language of the hand is discernible within the medical past. It was the 17th-century doctor John Bulwer who set out the origins of sign language in his enchanting book Chirologia, or the Naturall Language of the Hand (1644). He conceptualised the hand as a second mouth, so keen is its capacity to communicate by gesture and by sign. For Bulwer, it was the hand, not the mouth, that could speak a universal language, the ‘chiefest instrument of eloquence’. Two hundred years later, Bell, one of the greatest anatomists of his day, also wrote of the ‘eloquent’ hand. And a century after that, Wolff wrote about the psychoanalytic body that speaks, in A Psychology of Gesture (1945), placing her work on primate hands in just this tradition.

Today, some adventurous and imaginative medical schools take the connection between somatic signs, language and interpretation very seriously indeed, teaching physical examination through the idea of ‘The Body as Text’. ‘Every patient’s body tells a story,’ Stanford’s medical students are instructed. ‘The narrative includes the past and present of a person’s social and medical condition.’ Bulwer, Bell, Crookshank and Wolff would have added ‘and the future’: signs on the hand were not just diagnostic, but prognostic. The Stanford School of Medicine frames the physical examination as an old-school art that needs to be retained, not superseded, by various technologies that ‘see’ inside. This is the art, science and language of decoding the phenotype. It is quite right that Stanford explains this ‘body as text’ method as the interpretation of the phenotype. Yet when their clinicians teach this language of the body, they are perhaps unaware of just how long and distinguished the tradition of decoding somatic signs is.

When dead Mok’s hand first reached out to me – far more than a ghost – I was culturally cornered, stuck thinking that the palm was relevant only to palmistry. Yet of course the hand – including the fingerprints, the palm and its folds, creases and patterns – is plain human anatomy made semiotically and phenotypically meaningful. For centuries, fortune-telling palmists have studied the hand to unlock the future and the past, health and character, but so too have other experts in bodies and minds: physicians, psychologists, psychiatrists, embryologists, anatomists, endocrinologists, primatologists and physical anthropologists.

Having followed a language of the hand both backwards and forwards in time from Mok’s poignant print, it was especially affecting to learn that, as a medical elder in the 1970s, Penrose the curious geneticist was himself pursuing the history of palmistry: one of the final publications of his stellar career was on fingerprints and palmistry, published in The Lancet, no less. For me, Mok’s print became slowly unveiled from its occult state, no longer inscrutable and mysterious, but now known, legible, and clear, a historical secret disclosed.
